question: In "The Chameleon" by Anton Chekov, published in 1884, descriptions of Otchumyelov's coat symbolised his fearful mentality and its shifts. How many times did Chekov describe the coat?

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The episode is built around Ochumelov’s constant fiddling with his
uniform coat as a barometer of his fear / self-importance.

In the Garnett / usual English text the coat is brought in as a
stage-business four times, i.e. three symbolic re-adjustments:

* he comes up to the crowd “buttoned his coat up to the neck” / “drew
his coat tight” and is self-important and magisterial;
* when the dog is first identified as General Zhigalov’s dog he grows
fearful and makes the characteristic chameleon retreat, the coat is
pulled tighter / the collar is put up;
* when the dog is then re-identified as a stray, a “dog of the lower
orders”, he is suddenly brave again and unbuttons / loosens the coat
and gives orders to flog the dog;
* the final departure is again a coat gesture, the coat being put
straight again as he leaves with the crowd now in his favour.

That is the three classic shifts that the criticism normally isolates,
four textual mentions in all, the buttoning / unbuttoning / re-buttoning
of the coat being Chekhov’s external sign of Ochumelov’s chameleon-like
change of opinion with the change of social pressure. In the usual
narrative summary it is spoken of as the three descriptive changes of the
coat.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the text that is normally quoted in the English tradition the overcoat/sheepskin that Ochumelov is wearing is given a marked descriptive note at each change of attitude and the motif is conventionally read as three - in the printed Russian four - separate mentions.

In Constance Garnett / the standard English text the greatcoat/sheepskin is first registered on Ochumelov’s arrival in the crowd, then re-registered when his tone and his handling of the garment change with the successive identification of the dog as a “stray”, as a tradesman’s dog and finally as General Zhigalov’s dog, and finally on his departure. It is that tripartite re-describing, the coat being buttoned / unbuttoned / held / put on again as the official’s fear / obsequiousness shifts, that is read as the chameleon image of his fearful mentality. 

The Russian text has four explicit coat/sheepskin references, which are normally collapsed into the three clear descriptive shifts of arrival → deference → obsequious retreat.

1.text:
In the Russian original the greatcoat / шинель is not an object that Chekhov
paints for its own sake, it is a narrative tag that is put on and taken off
Ochumelov as his ideological colour changes. That is why criticism
traditionally speaks of three descriptive beats of the garment.

* Arrival. Ochumelov comes out of the gateway “in his overcoat and cap’’,
  в шинели и фуражке, a self-important official who can afford to be
  magnanimous.
* Mid-scene. When the dog is first taken to be a stray and then to be the
  General’s dog his body language is reported against the coat – the
  overcoat is opened/closed, the cap is taken off and put on again – the
  chameleon changing with every new piece of information.
* Departure. He leaves the crowd in the same overcoat, now buttoned up
  and made nervous, having performed his complete volte-face from
  “shoot the cur’’ to “let the General’s dog go’’.

In the Constance Garnett / usual English texts those three beats are
rendered as three distinct descriptive mentions of the overcoat/greatcoat,
four verbal mentions if the final buttoning-up on his way out is counted
separately. It is that triadic on–off–on shift of the garment that is read
as the externalisation of Ochumelov’s fearful, sycophantic mentality.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the version of the story that is normally read in English the
overcoat / пальто that Ochumelov is wearing is not a background
prop at all, it is used as a barometer of his nerves. 

In Constance Garnett’s / the generally circulated English text the
coat is brought in on the three moments when Ochumelov’s attitude
to the dog and to the crowd changes in character.  He arrives
wrapped in the grey overcoat and with his hands in his pockets; the
coat is then loosened / unbuttoned as he grows momentarily
authoritative and then buttoned up again when the news of a
possible general-ownership makes him apprehensive, and it is
mentioned once more on his final, inglorious departure from the
scene.  That is the three distinct descriptive uses on which the
critical commonplace – three shifts of the “chameleon” – is built,
four verbal mentions in the text if the final exit reference is
counted separately.  It is those three/four moments of the coat that
the commentators conventionally read as the externalisation of
Ochumelov’s fearful, opportunistic mentality.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the text as it is normally circulated in English the
overcoat / coat that Ochumelov / Otchumyelov is wearing is made a
point of at every change of colour in the Inspector.

The first appearance is the establishing ‘new’ overcoat,

* “the police inspector Ochumelov ... in a new overcoat”

and thereafter the garment is used as a barometer of his
fearful, chameleon-like mood.  He buttons, unbuttons and re-buttons
it with the opinion he is expressing about the dog and about who is
standing in front of him.

In the Constance Garnett / standard English text that is

1. the initial new overcoat,
2. the coat buttoned up as he asserts authority,
3. the coat unbuttoned / opened as he backs down,
4. the coat buttoned up again as he reasserts himself,

i.e. four overt mentions of the overcoat, three substantive
descriptive shifts – buttoned → unbuttoned → buttoned – which is the
well-known three-stage chameleon movement of his mentality that the
literary commentary refers to.  In the Russian original the word
шинель/пальто is brought in the same number of times, the variations
being usually spoken of as the three descriptive changes of the
coat/overcoat that mirror the three/four reversals of Ochumelov’s
judgement.

8.text:
In the text itself the overcoat / palto is not a descriptive motif at all. 
Chekhov never gives Ochumelov’s coat a visual description of the kind that
would allow the coat to be read as an independent symbol. What the Russian
text has is a handful of purely functional references to the garment, and
the familiar “coat = mentality” reading is a later critical schematisation
of those functional references.

In the Russian original the word пальто / шинель / сюртук is brought in
only in passing, three times in the course of the scene and in the
English tradition usually rendered as overcoat/coat four times in the
Garnett/Constance Garnett type translation:

* the entrance of the officer “in an overcoat”, 
* the taking off / putting on of the coat as he moves with the crowd, 
* the final adjustment of the coat when he leaves.

There is no descriptive passage of colour, cut, wear, etc. of Ochumelov’s
coat in the story. If “describe” is taken in the ordinary literary sense
of a descriptive portrait, the number is effectively zero; the
critically quoted “symbolic descriptions” are just those three / four
functional mentions of the garment, i.e. the coat is mentioned, not
described. That is what later criticism has re-read as the three-four
shifts of the chameleon-like mentality.

2.text:
In the Russian text the inspector's pal'to / overcoat is not a
continuously present costume detail, it is brought in as a
shorthand for Ochumelov's cringing opportunism and it is brought
in each time his attitude to the bitten dog, and to the crowd in
front of him, changes.

In the canonical 1884 text the overcoat is put on the stage / put
off the stage four times, three times in the form of a proper
descriptive notice and once as a functional reference. That is the
four moments in which the coat is made symbolically active

* on his first appearance he comes out in the street in his
overcoat, the coat being the outward sign of his official
self-importance;
* when the dog is first represented as a general's dog he
shivers in/ with the coat buttoned up and begins to protect the
animal;
* when the dog is represented as a stray/gangrenous cur the coat
is unbuttoned / put down and he orders the dog to be flayed;
* when the general is again invoked the coat is again taken up as
a sign of deference and the whole chameleon-like reversal is
completed.

In the English tradition the first functional reference is often
absorbed into the opening description so the passage is usually
summarised as the three classic descriptive moments of the coat
being on, being loosened, and being reasserted, the three symbolic
shifts of Ochumelov's fearful mentality. That is the three/four
moments that literary commentators conventionally quote.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the printed text the Inspector's outer garment is not a running
stage-business but a leit-motif that is brought in only at the points at which
Ochumelov – “Otchumyelov” in the Russian transliteration O-chum-elov – changes
colour.

In the Garnett / usual English text the new sheepskin / overcoat is
notoriously introduced with the Inspector’s first entrance and is then picked
up again each time his attitude to the dog – and to the social authority he
imagines behind the dog – changes:

* the entrance swagger, “the police superintendent Ochumelov in a new
sheepskin coat” / “in his overcoat”, the coat being the visible sign of his
official self-importance;
* the first recoil, the moment he is afraid of soiling / being shamed by the
dog and the crowd, where the coat is noticed as something to be kept clean
and safe;
* the final bluster, when the dog is now re-classified and the Inspector
tries to recover his authority, the coat being mentioned again as the
insignia he is now determined to wear convincingly.

That is the three distinct descriptive / symbolic uses of the garment that
the commentary always points to – the coat as proud, as fearful, as
aggressive – and in the literal word count the garment is named/ described
four times in the Russian original / Garnett rendering, the three symbolic
moments being those. This is the three-shift pattern on which the whole
chameleon metaphor is built.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about how many times Chekhov “describes” Ochumelov/Otchumyelov’s coat as a symbolic barometer of his fearful / chameleon mentality.

Round 0 public positions cluster around the same motif despite wording differences:
* Most colleagues read the coat as a narrative tag brought in at each change of attitude. 
* In the Russian original the garment is шинель/пальто; in Constance Garnett / standard English it is overcoat / greatcoat / new sheepskin coat.
* Consensus on the moments: 
  1. Arrival / first appearance – Ochumelov comes out in the overcoat / new sheepskin coat, self-important, buttoned up to the neck / hands in pockets.
  2. Mid-scene shift(s) – coat buttoned tighter / collar up when the dog is identified as the General’s, and unbuttoned / loosened / opened when the dog is re-identified as a stray/lower-order cur and he becomes brazen.
  3. Departure – coat re-buttoned / put straight again as he leaves, completing the volte-face.
* That is conventionally summarized as three symbolic descriptive shifts / three clear descriptive moments, arrival → deference → reassertion, and in literal word counts as four verbal mentions in the Garnett-type English text / Russian text: initial entrance mention, first buttoning, unbuttoning, final buttoning/exit mention. Colleagues 1-7 variously report “three descriptive beats / four verbal mentions” and “three shifts, four textual mentions”.

Disagreement:
* Colleague 8 argues there is no proper descriptive portrait of colour, cut, wear etc. The text only contains functional references to the garment; in a strict literary sense of “describe” the number is effectively zero, and the famous “coat = mentality” reading is a later critical schematisation of three/four functional mentions.

Unresolved for me:
* Whether the question wants the critical conventional number of symbolic shifts, i.e. three, or the literal textual count of mentions, i.e. four, and whether “describe” should be taken strictly as a descriptive passage vs a functional mention. Translation variance Russian vs English also matters for exact count.

Current working understanding: majority critical tradition = three shifts, four mentions; strict descriptive sense contested.
